And when I was questioned by the Prosecutor, I repeated that and stated it once again. And I should like to emphasise once again that I cannot comment on the contents of Mr. Bursik's report or notes. Call him into the courtroom for him to explain what he wrote, why he wrote it, the way he wrote it and how he understood it. Because I really can't comment on other people's notes. And it's very difficult to comment on them, and I don't think anybody will be able to comment on my own notes, what I thought at the time and what I understood and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we call your lawyers as well, since they were witnesses so they can testify under oath as to what you might have said and how the negotiations went on during that six-month period between them and the Prosecution? Can we call them?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether you have the right to call them and what rights you refer to. As far as I'm concerned, I am prepared to testify to all these matters further, and it is up to Their Honours if there is any need to call them in or not. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, we don't think it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think -- could I come to this conclusion: There's no difference or dispute concerning whether there's a meeting or not on the 12th of July. But there's a difference whether it's a normal, routine meeting or not. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Partly, Your Honour. Because it says the three of them, "as was their norm," giving the impression that the three of them every day were meeting. And that to me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I quite understand you. I quite understand you. I think you made your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. And I apologise for belabouring the point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at some point when it became necessary to speak with the Prosecution, you were advised by your lawyers that you needed to be truthful.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they certainly did not advise you to lie.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or to, perhaps, equivocate, not tell the whole truth?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karnavas. My lawyers advised me to tell the truth. They acquainted me with all my rights and duties. They advised me on all legal aspects in the matter. Everything, in fact, that comes under their competence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And they also went over the documents so at least you knew at that point what the Prosecution had in store for you if you went to trial.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my lawyers did send me that material in, all those documents, or most of the ones that the OTP disclosed to my lawyers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And you went over those documents with them?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course I did go through them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you met with an expert in your particular field?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have a meeting with an expert.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at some point, you began making statements to the Prosecutor. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And after that, we, or rather I began making the statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Exactly. And prior to making that statement, is it not a fact that you had been provided with a list of facts by the Prosecution as to what he believed you should admit to? Is that not a fact?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not true that I was given any list of facts before I entered into acceptance of responsibility or my guilty plea. We defined the facts about my acceptance of responsibility after lengthy discussions, and that's how we arrived at those facts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So at no time did the Prosecution through your lawyers tell them to impart to you the various facts that you needed to agree to and accept?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed many facts, the entirety of the case itself and all the different aspects of it. And we arrived at the conclusion that - that is to say, my lawyers and I, myself - came to the conclusion that these roughly were the facts as they stood, and that they should be then translated on to paper and written out in the form of a document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it not true that your lawyers, from their conversations and negotiations with the Prosecution, had a laundry list of facts that the Prosecution expected you to agree to or to accept in part or in whole as part of the negotiating process? Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not, Mr. Karnavas. No list at all was compiled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And they didn't tell you verbally what the Prosecution wanted to hear? They didn't say: "Say something about Blagojevic or there's no deal"? That never happened?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, pounding the table is not a proper manner, you know, especially in this courtroom. You have to show some respect to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, when you began speaking to the Prosecutor, you told them that you had participated in a massacre, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not how it was, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you not take responsibility for ordering the executions at Sandici and at the Kravica warehouse on July 13th, 1995? Did you not tell the Prosecutor that you had ordered those executions?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. At one point I did state that, and I wish, before this Honourable Trial Chamber, to explain why I said what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it. I didn't tell the truth when I said that. I myself without any influence from anybody made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our agreement in a period of time, in my assessment, could have fallen through. That was how I saw it. It might have fallen through, this agreement. And so I wanted at all costs to have this agreement between myself and the OTP stand. So I wanted to plead guilty, I wanted to accept my responsibility for the crime in Srebrenica and to recognise before this Trial Chamber that I took part in that particular crime. I wanted to take my part of the responsibility for that. So at that point in time, quite simply, I took on more than was my share and what I actually had done. After that, I apologised both to the Prosecutor and to my own lawyers and said that I had, indeed, made a mistake, that I had lied, that that was not the truth. I said -- I told the Prosecutor and my lawyers that I would in continuation of our conversation tell the truth in future. And that's what I did. So I take advantage of this opportunity here and now in this courtroom to apologise to Their Honours and the Honourable Trial Chamber for having done that, and to apologise to the Defence counsel for having done what I did with respect to Kravica and Sandici. And that is the whole truth as far as that matter is concerned, and that is the only falsehood that I told, that I uttered in the conversation that I had, that is to say, in the presence of my own Defence counsel and the Prosecutor. We continued our conversations, and I stand by everything I said after that. And I stand by it. That is the truth, and that is how it happened. And I want to say another thing. I want to tell Their Honours one more thing, and that is I wanted before this Honourable Trial Chamber to come and testify as a man who had recognised his guilt. I recognised and acknowledged that a crime had been committed, and I wanted to move the case of Srebrenica from the dead end it had come to. I wanted the truth to be heard, that you hear these words uttered from a man who was there and took part in it. That was my intention. I apologise once again to the Trial Chamber, to my Defence counsel, and to the Prosecutor for having uttered that falsehood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's stick with Tab B. Let's stick with your mistake which, in fact, was a lie, shall we? Now, at the time that you made this mistake, you knew you were lying, did you not? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. I confess that I wasn't telling the truth at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It wasn't some irresistible impulse that you could just not resist telling a lie; it was a calculated risk that you took --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, we do not use "lie," the word. We use "false statement" or something neutral.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand I'm in an International Tribunal. We're dealing with an execution. We're dealing with somebody who wanted a deal, was willing by his own testimony to say anything. He used the word "lie." I'm merely repeating what he has indicated. And I don't think in my humble opinion using diplomatic niceties to call it a falsehood when in fact it is a bald-faced lie, I don't think we do a service to the international community. We should call it for what it is. But if the Court wishes me to call it a falsehood, I will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, the witness has already admitted he made a mistake. No matter if you call it a lie or false statement, there is no difference. But this is an International Tribunal, and you are a professional. So can you accept our suggestion that you use the word "false statement."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you made this false statement, you had decided that you were going to take a risk, had you not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you just tell me which document you're looking at?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm looking at --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the statement before me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your declaration. We're going to stay with this.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have the declaration in front of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. When you made -- but I'm not interested in what you declared after the falsehood; what I'm interested in is the mental process that went through in conceiving and executing the falsehood. So if I recall, earlier, you stated that part of your profession required you to use deceptive measures, or take deceptive measures as an intelligence officer. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right, Mr. Karnavas. And I didn't say at all what you're now claiming I did. What I said was this: That one of the ways, one of the methods employed, one of the methods of work was, amongst others, to represent yourself to members of foreign armed forces, as far as that was possible, rather, to conceal your role, function, and post. That is a component part of intelligence work, or rather security staff. And that is something that is allowed. I never uttered the sentence you have just said. So I explained exactly how this is done, why this is done, what the purpose of it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you represented yourself to be a major when, in fact, you were not even a captain first-class, that was a falsehood, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should like to ask Their Honours to allow me to explain how this came about in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, we Judges are also interested in the mental process when you tell the Prosecution something that is not true. Can you explain that. Because Mr. Karnavas asked this question, then he changed to another subject. I think we should concentrate on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I was getting around to it, but I agree with you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us the mental process that went through, how you sit down and you conceive, plan, and then execute a convincing falsehood, based on your experiences.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, all I can do is to confess and say that the conversation about the crime, the discussion about the crime, and acceptance of the crime, confessing to it is a very difficult situation to be in. And anybody who finds himself in a situation of that kind, of having to talk about it does not feel at all, if I say comfortable, that's a mild word. But what you feel is quite simply -- you feel yourself to be somebody who confesses to carrying out something and taking part in something which was, in fact, a crime. So this is not a pleasant task. It is not a situation in which one feels comfortable or normal in. And it is not pleasant. I can't seem to find a different term to express my sentiments on that score. I also wish to say that my feelings and sentiments at that point in time --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Were quite simply, as I was saying, quite simply at that point in time, or rather up until that point, I had confessed to my faults. I talked about many difficult matters. And all this took me back and reminded me of the period of time when this actually happened, when it took place. So I felt very uncomfortable, and I could not, in full, control the chronology of events, the chronology of what I was saying. Quite simply, there were no preparations beforehand in the sense of my preparing myself. It just came about during the conversation. The Prosecutor asked me what happened in Sandici. I said what I said. He said: "Did you take part in what happened in Kravica?" I said: "Yes, I did." And then what happened came about. I said what I said. So that was during this questioning. After several hours of work, several hours of questioning, quite simply, I stated what I did, and we had a break after that. I then met with my lawyers, and I realised what I had done. I think that this was more out of despair, desperation, rather than having given much thought to it. And quite simply, that's what I went through. That is the process I went through when we come to discussing this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Karnavas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now there was a particular photograph that you believed depicted you in it. And you're shaking your head, so I take it you understand English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, it's a statement, not a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Where is your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question is that initially, you stated that you were in a photograph in the area of Sandici. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time, you believed that was you, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You truly believed that that was Momir Nikolic in looking at that particular picture?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did believe that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that -- I take it, then, that you must have been at Sandici at the time when you are purportedly being depicted in this particular photograph?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karnavas. I confessed that I was on that route twice on the 13th. And regardless of remembering the details that took place when I passed along that way, I quite simply was not able to exclude the possibility of getting out of the vehicle at that point in time, that I was photographed, and that I was actually there. So I was there on the 13th the first time, and a second time, and quite possibly I did step out of the car and happen to find myself in that part of Sandici when somebody took a photograph of me. So that's what I told the Prosecutor, and my lawyers, too. Now, afterwards, later on, my lawyers conducted an investigation because they doubted whether it was actually me on the photograph. So an investigation was conducted, and my lawyers at one point investigated this matter of the photograph and uncovered the person who was actually on the photograph. The photograph and person was taken in profile. We can take a look at it together. He does resemble me in profile, because I had a moustache during the war so we can take a look at the photograph all together, because the person really does resemble me, so that's why I thought and said that it was, in fact, me. And when we conducted this investigation, we established, rather my lawyers established, that it was somebody quite different, another man who was there. We have disclosed and discovered his identity. He confessed that it was him. He said yes, indeed it was, so this dispersed all doubts as to whether it was me on the photograph or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was your lawyers, according to you, who had the doubts, not Momir Nikolic, and that is why they went and did the investigation. Is that your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I said that I had doubts, together with them. But that I did not at any point in time exclude the possibility of it -- of I myself having been in the area at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's get back to the Kravica warehouse. I'm still a little confused. How is it that you thought that by admitting to the -- to one of the most horrendous executions that had ever taken place in this area, that that would help you with the Prosecution and with the Trial Chamber in getting the kind of sentence that you're hoping and praying for?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karnavas. At the time, I did not -- my thinking process wasn't the kind you've just described. I did mind, and I wanted the agreement to be successful, to come about. I did not want to go to trial. And in my assessment, it was my assessment that everything that took place in Srebrenica, the crime that took place there, that nobody, including myself, could avoid responsibility and their guilt. And that the Prosecution has at its disposal documents which absolutely do indicate the participation of my unit, the unit in which I was the chief of the security intelligence organ. And on the basis of this overall weighing up of the matter, I came to realise that the best solution for me personally would be to enter into an agreement of this kind, to come before the Trial Chamber, to confess my guilt, to testify about the crime. And in that way, quite simply, to save myself, that is to say, not to have to go through something that I already went through during the war. That on the one side, and on the other, to help the Court to arrive at the truth as far as that is possible. So those were the reasons that guided me. I have no others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, you were trying also to assist the Prosecution in solving a piece of the puzzle. Who ordered the massacre? And if Momir Nikolic could step up to the plate and take responsibility, in the Prosecution's eyes, he would have solved at least one piece of the puzzle that was still missing, and then you could get the sort of benefit that you're hoping and praying for from this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, it's not a question. Ask your question instead of statement. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I was just going to suggest that baseball is a great game, but I'm not sure it's going to help this guy in answering the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think the previous question was very good, was very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, did you think that by admitting, falsely admitting, to having ordered this execution, that you were solving a question mark in the Prosecution's case as to who, in fact, had ordered that massacre? Is that what you were trying to do when you made the admission?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say, Mr. Karnavas, is that at that point in time I really didn't think along those lines, as to whether I would solve anything by that statement. I made that statement. I said that. And I cannot now speculate with it as to what I had in mind, whether I would solve anything or not. I really didn't think about that at all most probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you picked that particular crime, not, say, Branjevo farm where there was another execution. You picked that one. You selected that particular atrocious incident in the history of mankind to accept responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I didn't select that crime, nor did I select it. We started discussing it simply. And that is the only crime as far as I know of that kind in view of the way in which it was committed. That is, in Kravica. So my answer is I didn't select that crime. We discussed it. And I said what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in discussing it, was not the Prosecutor implying through his questions - I wasn't there, I don't have a tape recorder; wish I did - but was he not implying that perhaps Momir Nikolic, chief of intelligence and security of the Bratunac Brigade, was involved, instrumental in that particular massacre as well as in Sandici?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karnavas. The Prosecutor did not in any way suggest or require me to say that. Through a very correct conversation, we reached that issue. And as I have already explained to you, why and for what reasons I said what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I know, Your Honour, we're ready for a break, but I would like to go for a few more moments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not insinuating that he tried to get you to say anything wrong but I am ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's another statement, and of course, it was exactly what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But, Mr. McCloskey, you have to understand that Defence counsel has the right to ask any questions that are in the interests of his client. I think this is a particular case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the questioning by Mr. McCloskey, did it appear to you that Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Bursik thought, suspected that Momir Nikolic was involved in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot claim anything with that respect, that is, whether Mr. McCloskey or Mr. Bursik thought that, what their assessment was. I really don't know what Mr. McCloskey thought about it, and I don't know what Mr. Bursik thought about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the conversation was about Kravica, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you raise it? Did you say: "Now, Mr. McCloskey, let's get into Kravica," or was it Mr. McCloskey directing the line of questioning, telling you that he wished to discuss this particular massacre with you? Who was leading whom?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Karnavas, it was the Prosecutor who was leading the conversation, and I was answering questions. And the question of Kravica came up as a normal question in the chronology of events on the 13th, that is, when I returned from Konjevic Polje. So it was nothing outside the chronology of the questions put by Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you knew at the time that the questions were being posed, that he, Mr. McCloskey, was interested in solving that mystery; that is, who ordered, who specifically ordered, the massacre in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only assume so, that the Prosecutor was interested in all the details and all the facts and everything. That could be said with reference to all the crimes, including the crime in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, one last -- if we could go back to the information report, the one that we discussed earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And for the record, we're discussing D29/1 for identification purposes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's on page 8 on the English version. And it's the seventh paragraph from the top down. So it would have been four paragraphs down from the one where we earlier discussed. And if I could just help you out here, it begins with saying: "Nikolic states that he was at the Kravica warehouse on the 13th July (later retracted this) and ordered the execution there." If you could find that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And then you go on -- at least, according to Mr. Bursik. He says that you said: "He said that Borovcanin arrived whilst the execution was underway, and they spoke about what they should do about the bodies of those executed." Right? That's what it says?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, now --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what it says. But that is not what I said with regard to Borovcanin. I said --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may interrupt --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Certain things about Borovcanin, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, this is a very important piece of the evidence. We would like to know the details. So you have to allow the witness to give some explanations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I totally agree, Your Honour. And I would be more than happy to have him give an explanation, but after at least he answers my question. But I agree. I will -- we'll go this route. We'll go this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Nikolic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. At the time I was speaking about the -- Kravica in general, I said that I had information. I didn't put it the way it is stated here, that Mr. Borovcanin was there during the execution, that he knew about everything that was going on. I spoke about the reasons for the execution, why it took place, and the other details that I learned about after everything that had happened. So the way it is written here is not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it goes on to say that actually with regard to the incident, the guard that had been killed and so on. I did speak about that. Now, what Mr. Bursik put down, I really don't know. I don't know how he understood what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, if the Defence counsel needs more information, he will ask questions to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, so Mr. Nikolic, what you're saying here today right now is that this paragraph, as it is written, is incorrect at best, false at worst?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that. I just said that it is not written in the way I said it in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me read the second sentence here. It says: "He said that Borovcanin arrived whilst the execution was underway, and they spoke about what they should do about the bodies of those executed." Now, you claim today, and we have no reason to know, but you claim today that that is not what you said in the presence of Mr. McCloskey and your lawyers. Is that correct? You didn't say this?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regard to the execution and the discussion about the bodies of those executed, I think that we didn't talk along those lines. But rather, I said that I had knowledge as to what had happened with the bodies of the people who were executed, and that Ljubisa Borovcanin was included and that he knew what was happening in that respect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you had knowledge, you had obtained knowledge either beforehand or through the documents provided to you that Borovcanin was there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you put that knowledge that you had into your little fact pattern when you -- into the facts that you were outlining as far as how you were there in Kravica ordering the executions. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that I, too, though I wasn't involved there, that I was involved in that part of the events in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And of course, that was false.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I wasn't in Kravica. After having admitted the error, I said that I was never in Kravica, and that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you included Borovcanin into your story, into your falsehood, in order to make your falsehood or your story convincing enough to the Prosecution so that he could buy it. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not include Borovcanin in the story in the way it is written here. I knew how Borovcanin was involved in this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were never present in Kravica, according to your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my testimony, I was not in Kravica during the execution of this crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And then you state that Borovcanin did nothing to prevent the shooting that you had ordered. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that. The question was whether I did anything, having admitted that I had ordered it, I said -- then the question was with regard to Borovcanin, and I said that I did nothing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, but you're saying that he did nothing. "Borovcanin did nothing to stop the shooting while he was there." You've included him into your story through this line, that he was there with you, and he did nothing to stop the execution. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I knew that Borovcanin was not there, so I knew that. And apart from my involvement, the rest is true. He was there, and he did nothing. And I know that on the basis of information I collected later, after the execution. So I know that he did nothing to stop it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you collected information, and you read information. And based on that information, you came up with a story that you could sell to the Prosecution. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that I included myself, or rather I admitted to participating over there, but that most of what is there is correct, and it did take place according to my information. So my error and what is not correct is my participation in all that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said you collected information. You did an investigation on Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I am not an authorised person for any kind of investigation. I just collected information about what was happening -- what happened in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, it goes on to say that "During the time, women and children were passing by in buses." Does it not say that, the last sentence?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that, too--

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's a fact?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is something that is correct, and it is true that according to my knowledge, when this crime was committed, buses were passing along that road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in concocting, in creating, in formulating, in designing a falsehood, you, Momir Nikolic, took some information which you knew to be true or factual, believable, provable, and incorporated that information into your -- into the falsehood in order to give your story more believability?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karnavas. I included myself in all this for the reasons that I have already explained. And everything else that is written here, among other things, are things that happened about which I had information that they had happened. I had confirmation that they had happened on that day or those days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the falsehood, the false information that was contained in the story was about yourself. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The false part of the statement relates to my participation in that operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rest, regarding the participation of Borovcanin and the other details linked to the -- how the murder came about, the information about the incident, I knew about that, and that information is quite correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But getting back to what I said, the false information in this story relates to Nikolic, and Nikolic stood to gain the most from the story that Nikolic himself had created and served to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not, Mr. Karnavas, at that point in time think along those lines, as to what I would gain and what I would lose. Just then I had decided, since the Prosecution and I were in an advanced stage, and since I had conveyed to the Prosecution everything that I had done and I had been involved in, I simply felt that the agreement should be signed with the Prosecution, and that that agreement should be reached, that I should confess my guilt and plead guilty. And within that framework, I made this error, and that is all I can say now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, first I want to thank everyone here for going beyond the normal breaking period. And I think this would be a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will resume at 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we leave Tab B, I'd like to recall your attention, Mr. Nikolic, to what you stated back on Friday, 19 September 2003, transcript page 1595. You stated, and I'm quoting from lines 9 through to 11: "Once the agreement with the Prosecution had already advanced, I came to the decision that there would be no agreement, and I really wanted to obtain an agreement." Do you recall making that statement on Friday in this courtroom? That was Friday, the 19th, September 19th.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, Mr. Karnavas, what I said on Friday. And what I said was that when conversations between me and the Prosecution were in an advanced stage, I simply made an assessment. My personal assessment was that the agreement could be called in question. And I feared that that might happen because I had already told the Prosecutor and those present most of what -- I had arguments to offer, and I believed that an agreement should be reached and that at that point in time, that was the best solution for me, and that is why I made that decision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you acknowledge today stating back on Friday, the 19th September 2003, as it states here on page 1595, on line 10: "I came to the decision that there would be no agreement, and I really wanted to obtain an agreement." You recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure. Really, I can't remember exactly each and every sentence. But if that is what it says in the transcript, then that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And just for the record, I also believe a line of answers in this respect were noted today, and I'm told as on page 48.12, and it was approximately 11:40:19. Now, may I ask, Mr. Nikolic, what was it that led you into believing, into having these feelings, that perhaps an agreement would not be reached?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just then, I really didn't make any analyses or calculations as to why the agreement may not be reached. That was just the impression I had just then at that point in time. Those were the feelings I had. And this was a terrible period for me. I don't even wish to remember it, never mind talk about it. And I was admitting to something that really is hard. It was the crime that happened in Srebrenica. It is not easy to talk about it, nor was it easy to confess to one's involvement in such a crime. And all these circumstances created the impression in my mind that there could be some misunderstanding. And to be quite frank, I was convinced that most of what I had been saying to the Prosecution, that the Prosecution already has the facts and circumstances about all that. And all these were factors that prompted me to come to the conclusion that all this may not be sufficient for an agreement. It was along those lines that my thoughts went at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You thought the Prosecutor had all the facts that you could give him, and you needed to give him something that he did not have, something that you could come up with to satisfy his needs and, of course, your needs as well. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite, Mr. Karnavas. I simply at the time made such a decision. And all this -- these circumstances and the set of circumstances surrounding the crime, the confession, my role, and everything that happened in Srebrenica and around Srebrenica were always present in my mind, and I simply did not wish to have to go through that process again, not to have to go on trial. I wanted to admit my guilt, and I simply wanted to cooperate with the Prosecution. That was my decision. And I wish to tell Their Honours and to admit here that it is quite normal that I expected because I would come out and confess to all that, that I would make it easier for myself, the Prosecution, and the Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't that you just wanted to get it over with, you also expected to benefit. You wanted to limit your time, imprisonment, to 20 years. Right? That was part of the arrangement? Quid pro quo.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, my lawyers set before me all the ways and means and all the rights that I enjoy before this Tribunal. They told me everything that I could expect, in all the different variations, all the different possibilities, and what would happen if I went to trial, what would happen if I pleaded guilty, and so on. So they explained all the different ways in which I could get through this process. And it was I who decided. They didn't wield any influence on my final decision. I was the one who made the final decision, and I decided to enter into this agreement and to act in the way I have acted. So nobody else wielded any essential influence on me except for the fact that my lawyers did explain to me all the different legal options before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And vis-a-vis this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one of the things that you wanted to enjoy was the right or I guess we would call it privilege to walk the earth a free person, spend time with your family, and not to have somebody tell you when you will wake up, what you will eat, when you will have your one-hour walk in a confined, caged -- in a prison setting. Right? Am I not correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, you are quite right in saying that everybody, all people, including myself, would like all this to last as short as time as possible. But what I also want to tell you is that regardless of the fact that I do wish to get out of here as soon as possible, to be reunited with my family, in this process, in this trial, I have conjured up the strength to -- and plucked up the courage to acknowledge and admit why I'm here, which means that I decided to take the hard road. I have decided to acknowledge and confess to my mistake, to confess to the crime. And that I think that I am the first officer from the Army of Republika Srpska who was a participant and yet admits to everything, confesses to all the things that he took part in. And quite simply, in admitting to my guilt and in admitting my participation, in confessing to that, I am fully conscious of the fact that I will pay and be punished for my mistake. And I don't see anything inhuman in that, the fact that I have accepted to talk about this, to testify about it. And let me just also tell you, Mr. Karnavas, this: In this process, in this trial, I am not testifying against anybody. I am testifying about the events that took place in Srebrenica. I am testifying about my participation in them. And I am not sparing anybody here, and not myself either. So that was the final decision, and that was what made me make it and decide to testify here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you thought there would be no deal, because the Prosecution had all the facts that you could give him, you needed to give him some more facts to sweeten the deal so that he would go ahead and make the arrangements that have been made here today. And that's why you provided this story, this falsehood, about Kravica. Right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I've already said several times that it was not the Prosecution who insisted upon this. The Prosecution did not ask that of me. The Prosecution did not exert any influence on me so that I should say that. My lawyers, likewise, did nothing along those lines to make me make the decision I made. So what I did is my own mistake. I have admitted it here, confessed to it. And there's nothing more I can say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In an earlier question, I asked you whether you conducted an investigation with respect to Kravica. And I believe you indicated that you were not an authorised person to conduct such an investigation. Did I hear that answer correctly?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You heard it correctly. You heard my answer correctly, that the intelligence and security organ in the Light Infantry Brigade was not the officially authorised person or body to conduct any kind of investigation because investigations of that kind can only be carried out by officially authorised persons, which I was not. All I could do was gather information about it all, and that's what I did. I gathered information about that particular case, and all other cases which occurred during the war and were of interest or which came under the realm of my field of work. So I was not the officially authorised person. And let me make this clearer: Officially authorised persons were the chiefs of security, for example, in infantry brigades and higher units. I, myself, in the intelligence field conducted command and staff security which you could see from the guidelines and instructions we had here. So that I didn't conduct an investigation, I didn't have the power to do so, the authority to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could just for one last time hopefully go to what has been marked as P84 for identification purposes. I'm referring to the rules of service of security organs. And sir, if you could look at paragraph or article, I guess it would be, 43, and then also read 51 and 52.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Karnavas. You said paragraph 43. And which others?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then paragraph numbered 51 and 52.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. I have had a look at it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on 43, you went through Article number 43 or paragraph number 43, it states: "In the case of crimes that are within the competence of military courts and are prosecuted ex officio under the conditions prescribed by the law that regulates criminal procedure authorised officers of security organs may arrest a person and deliver him without delay to an investigative judge or military court or the nearest military unit or military institution." Is that what paragraph or Article 43 states?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it states.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have the authority to arrest someone and deliver him -- as it stated in here, to the investigative judge of a military court?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karnavas. I've already explained that in my response a moment ago. The right to take into custody or to arrest anybody is a right that authorised organs of security have, and the first level where this authorised organ of security exists is the security organ in the infantry brigade. And it is these organs as opposed to security intelligence organs that have official ID cards and badges. And this distinguishes them from the security intelligence organises in the light infantry brigades. I was not an official, authorised person bearing these ID cards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or badges. But I was an individual who was able to gather information about crimes perpetrated that come under the jurisdiction of the military courts and which are being prosecuted ex officio and which relate to the theft of weapons, the destruction of ammunition, the destruction of mines and explosives. So that is the realm and area in which it was my task to gather information and intelligence and to send them to the prosecution organs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, are you suggesting here that you could not use the military police to arrest someone, for instance, for not reporting to duty, leaving his post? Is that what you're suggesting here today? You did not have that authority? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I'm saying. But I have to say -- actually I have to give you an explanation because what I've said is not sufficient. I don't say that I did not have the authority to monitor the work of the military police and its services when arrests were being made of recruits or conscripts that had fled from the units. Had I had the duty to monitor the execution of those tasks, and those tasks are defined and orders issued by the brigade commander, whereas the leader, the commander of the military police following instructions and the rules of the military police is the authorised individual who does have the right to file a criminal report. So there are two cases -- there are two cases in which the commander of the military police can file a criminal report. The first case is having received permission from the commanding officer of the unit. And the other instance is when this is required, when it's an urgent case, and when criminal reports are required. But after a report of that kind is filed, he must inform the commander of his unit, the unit of which he is a member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Go to Article 51, and then 52. Just read them.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read it, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it it's your testimony after having read those that you still had no authority to investigate the crime such as the Kravica massacre to which you have falsely, at least at one point, admitted to ordering?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I told you quite specifically what my duties were because you asked me about the article defining crimes which came under the jurisdiction of military courts and which are prosecuted ex officio. That's what you asked me a moment ago. And this particular article, or rather paragraph 51, I can comment on it, but it would boil down to the answer I gave to your previous question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That you had no authority to initiate an investigation of a massacre such as Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have the authority to initiate an investigation, but I was duty-bound and did have the authority to gather information and data about what had happened in Kravica. And once I had done that, I was to inform the corresponding organ in the Bratunac Brigade who would then process this information and file a criminal report. And if Their Honours would allow me, may I say that I have here the reports filed, dated 1992 to 1995. And from those documents, you can see who files a criminal report, who signs these criminal reports and so on. So I do have the criminal reports with me, not all of them, of course, but a sufficient number for you to be able to see this chain and how the links in the chain go down to the actual filing of a report and so on, up to 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Needless to say, can we conclude that you did not exercise your authority to gather the information and then pass it on to the higher authorities in order for something to be done with respect to Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I want to say is this: I had information as to what had happened at Kravica. That same information was something that the organs dealing with investigations also had, and the organs who filed criminal reports. So this same information was something that the higher organs had, the superior authority also dealing in affairs of this kind. And they are officially authorised persons, which I was not. That's what I want to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the answer to my question is no.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer to your question is that I used and did what I was authorised to do. What you said, I was not authorised to do and therefore didn't do those things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. We'll move on. I would like to now show you what will be marked as D36/1 for identification purposes. I have the copies for the Chamber myself. The front page is in English, the second page is in Srpski or B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: For the record it has a number on top. 0308284 -- 03082452, a document we received from the Office of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could look at the second page, and please read it.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was provided --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was provided to us by the Office of the Prosecution. I can only assume that your lawyers also received it. Do you know whether they shared this information with you, this information?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I had this information among the documents that my lawyers gave me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you go over this document with your lawyers, if you recall, prior to, during, or after your numerous negotiating sessions that you were holding with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when we actually went over this document. All I can say is that I and my lawyers did take a look at this document together, that subsequently I also had a look at it in the Detention Unit, in my room there. I can't say, I can't give you an exact answer as to when I actually received this document. And whether it was before, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And from this document, do you recognise the name, at least, at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if you mean what's written down in handwriting, D. Vasic is the signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who is Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragomir Vasic is the head of the centre of the services of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Centre of which services? Maybe there was something lost in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the centre of the services of public security or the security services. I don't know what the actual heading was. But I know it was a centre of MUP in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And at the top of the page, on the first line, it refers to a Tomo Kovac. Have you ever come across that name before?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard of this name, Tomo Kovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who is Mr. Tomo Kovac?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tomo Kovac was one of the senior officers in MUP. Now, whether at that point in time he was the acting minister or the minister, I really can't say. But I do know that he was from the MUP, Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, having read this document prior to coming here today, and then reading it again today, does this document not refer to the incident in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this document refers to a series of incidents from the arrest of individuals, and then others, too. So there are a series of incidents which the document describes. Among others, it does refer to Kravica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Okay. Well, let's focus on Kravica, shall we? Now, would it be fair to say that what is being described in this document is rather different than what you have described to us during your direct examination? Is that not a fact?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not. I did not describe the incident as it took place. That means that I mentioned as far as I remember saying -- I mentioned saying that I knew the incident had taken place and that there was a soldier or officer involved with the seizing of a rifle and the killing of a member of the MUP. And I also said that as far as I knew, that was the main reason for which the mass killing in Oka [phoen] took place. That's roughly what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it not also state -- does it not state in this particular document that it was General Mladic who, after receiving a message from the field concerning an incident in Kravica, ordered that all POWs be liquidated? Is that not what this document states?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what it says, Mr. Karnavas. But before I read this document, never before did I ever hear of anything like this. So that means I don't know what was going on in Vlasenica, what orders were issued, who they were issued to, who received the information. I really know nothing about that, any of that, because that was going on 50 kilometres away from Bratunac, and I didn't know about what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I take it you can neither nor deny the accuracy of what is contained in this particular document which we received from the Prosecution that was addressed to them from Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm anything from this document. I can't confirm it or deny it. It's a document. I have nothing here. I don't know who wrote it, where it came from, who it was addressed to, who was informed. I have nothing, no grounds for me to be able to comment along those lines. So I don't know. I don't know who sent it. Actually, I don't know anything about it. It's a piece of paper without a heading, without anything else. It is signed by hand at the bottom. But other than that, I can't really say anything about it. I'm don't know the details. I'm not quite clear on the specifics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. We'll move on. Now, going back to Friday, 19th September 2003, back again to page 1595, you were asked a question, and this is on line 22: "Do you understand today and throughout the rest of your testimony how critically important it is for you to tell the whole truth?" Do you recall being asked that question?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which question, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question that was posed to you by the Prosecutor. "Do you understand today and throughout the rest of your testimony how critically important it is for you to tell the whole truth?"

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, that had been part of the agreement that you had been -- that you had reached with the Prosecutor earlier, that you would testify truthfully and tell the whole truth; not just some of it, but the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I said I told the truth to the best of my recollection. And I did so regarding the points I was asked about by the Prosecutor and also in response to questions put by you over the past three days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, on page 1598, that would be about three pages later, you're being asked about your background, and you indicated on page 10 -- I mean, on line 10: "And then after a year at the assembly, I was again appointed as director of the Kartonaza Bratunac company. I remained there until privatisation occurred. And after the privatisation had been carried out, I was unemployed again, and that was the period during which I was arrested." I've just read from lines 10 to line 14 of the transcript from September 19, 2003. Mr. Nikolic, do you recall making that statement?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke about my CV. And among other things, I mentioned that as well. And maybe I forgot to mention something, and that is that I was the old director of Kartonaza, and that after privatisation, I remained, I really don't know for how long, but I remained there and was elected by the owner to be the new director of Kartonaza. And holding that position of director of the new company which was no longer called Kartonaza, I stayed in that position for three or four months. I don't know exactly. If you have the figures, please remind me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So now you supplemented your answer. Do you wish to supplement anything more regarding that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding Kartonaza? There are many things that I could say, but will you please ask me what you're interested in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what I'm interested to know is why you have failed to inform us that you were fired, you were fired, not that after privatisation, you became unemployed. But you were fired from your position. Is that not a fact?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is absolutely not true. Not a single word of what you said is right. And if Their Honours allow it, I will give you a complete answer to this question as to why I left Kartonaza.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may conduct a correct examination, Your Honour, I do have some documents that I wish to put forward to the witness. And in doing so, he can give his explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I can show you what has been marked for identification purposes as D26/1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please get a better photocopy because I really can't see anything on this one. I can't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may confer with my colleague for one second, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can now. I'm sorry, I can read everything I have now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you could please look at it, at the top of the page, it designates "SM-PRO." And I do have the documents. We'll go through them. But since we're focussing on this particular document, is it fair to say that that was the new name of Kartonaza when it went from state ownership to private ownership?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One could say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And it's Bratunac, December 29, 2000. Do you see that? That was the date.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And then it states that this is a decision, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page, there seems to be a signature. We can't read the signature, but I believe it is signed by an Alempic, J., with the SM-PRO seal affixed to it. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to focus you on the part which says "explanation." "Starting with November 25, 2000, the employee from the pronouncement of this decision assigned to the position of the manager of the enterprise stopped appearing at his place of employment. As it is obvious that the aforementioned person no longer wishes to be employed with the employer, and as the requirements have been met to apply provisions of Article 91, item 8, the employer decided as in the pronouncement of the decision." Do you read that explanation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the top of the decision, it denotes that you cease to be an employee with this enterprise, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to show you some other documents with respect to Kartonaza when it was still called that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, would you please tell us the source of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The source. We went -- I had my investigator, Your Honour, collect all of these documents in the process of investigation. Everything was done by -- in accordance with the appropriate manner, and I have a letter here dated to me. I made a request, formal request in writing. And based on that request, these documents were provided to us. And if the Court wishes something more formal from -- a more formal source, we can provide that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I could show you what has been marked D27/1 for identification purposes. And along with that, why don't you look at -- can we give Mr. Nikolic also D23, D24, and D25. So 27, 23, 24, 25, and I truly apologise for not having the numbering in a better system. I take full responsibility for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, it seems to me that you could not finish the cross-examination before the time. So could we continue in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Because, you know, we have just been furnished with so many documents at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just lost track of time, Your Honour. But absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We have to stop on time during this period because of the lunch break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, all right. I was under the wrong assumption, Your Honour, that we would keep going. But very well, this would be a very good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps if the witness could be provided with these documents, he could look at them so we could save some time in the afternoon because it looks like there's a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. We'll provide him with all the documents. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, so we'll resume at 3.00 this afternoon. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.43 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, you have something to address to the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. While we were on our lunch break, I received a fax, two faxes, in fact, from my investigator Risto Lugonic. Last night, yesterday afternoon, I asked him to go down to Bratunac and try to locate and meet with one particular witness, or an individual that has been named by Mr. Nikolic. The individual's name is Mile Petrovic. This is a gentleman that Mr. Nikolic asserts has -- was the one that picked up six Muslims and then executed them, and then came back and said: "Boss, I took revenge for my brother." I think the Court may recall that testimony. I had met the gentleman on a prior occasion with my investigator and with Ms. Tomanovic, so he had flatly denied that. So last night, I thought in light of the testimony, that we would contact him and ask if he would provide us with a -- that he would be interviewed by my investigator, be posed certain questions, and to see whether he would be willing to come to The Hague and testify. Through my investigator, we had learned -- we learned that on 25th of August, 2003, which would have been subsequent to the change of plea hearing when it was live and covered throughout Bosnia, especially on the television station in the Federation, the statement of facts became known. And as a result of that, this particular gentleman was taken to the police station of Bratunac, and he provided a statement. And with me, I have the minutes from the statements of -- of the questioning process that took place on the 25th of August, 2003. So I have two documents: One, I have a letter from my investigator dated today, faxed today. And it indicates that it was received at 12.26 p.m. It indicates that, one, that the individual flatly denies the allegations. Secondly, that the gentleman was approached by the Defence team of Mr. Nikolic and was requested to provide a statement that might be helpful to Mr. Nikolic. This particular witness declined, unable to providing anything concretely that would be of assistance to Mr. Nikolic. And there is a paragraph on page 3 where the witness believes that because of his refusal to provide this statement, that perhaps that may be one of the reasons, the motives, for Mr. Nikolic now claiming that six individuals were picked up of which he killed, and then later on he came back and said: "Boss, I took revenge." He does acknowledge being in the APC, although slight -- there's a difference in the way he describes it. And also indicates that two Muslims were picked up, one of which was physically abused by none other than Momir Nikolic. So in light of this, I should also note that recently, within the last day or so, the individual that has been assisting us in translating abruptly tendered her resignation, probably because of the amount of work that we have been -- and the deadlines imposed on her. So we don't have the capabilities of translating this. I do believe this is vital, that I need to confront this particular witness because I would recall to the Court's attention the joint motion for consideration of the amended plea agreement in which on paragraph 11, which -- and this was agreed upon by all the parties, it indicates, and I read: "It is understood and agreed by Momir Nikolic and the Prosecution that all information and testimony provided by Mr. Nikolic must be absolutely truthful. This means that Momir Nikolic must neither minimise his own actions, nor fabricate," nor fabricate, and I underscore that, "someone else's involvement." It would appear to us from this at this stage that we have some conflicting testimony. The individual is prepared to come to the Hague. It states it quite clearly here. He is in Bratunac at this time. In other words, he has been available to the Prosecution, had the Prosecution wished to check out this information. I don't know, maybe they have, maybe they haven't. In any event, I think in light of this, I would be requesting the following: One, assistance from the Trial Chamber to see whether either through the OTP or through the registry we could get these documents translated on an expedited basis. I cannot do proper cross-examination if I cannot, first of all, read it, and also I may need to go back and forth with respect to the documents. I think it's vital that I confront this witness and give him an opportunity to explain to the Tribunal, to the Trial Chamber his version of the events, again, if necessary, and perhaps to agree, deny, or whatever. But I think it's very important that I lock this person into his testimony, now that I have this information. And I think I'm duty-bound, I'm duty-bound to ensure that Mr. Blagojevic gets a fair trial which would include full rights under the Statute with respect to, I believe it's Article 21 or 20 which talks about the right to confrontation. And I can think of no, no greater importance at this stage in these proceedings than to allow us the opportunity to confront this particular witness who has had, might I add, and I'm sure I've said this in the past, plenty of opportunities, days and days and days of proofing sessions, negotiations, meetings with the Prosecution, and so on and so forth. So I think it is a reasonable request. So I would ask that while we proceed this afternoon, that whatever you could do, Mr. President and Your Honours, to assist us in getting these documents translated so I can go into this. While I'm at it, I can say with a great deal of certainty, and I'm sad to say this, but I will say it anyway, but there's no way humanly possible that I can finish my cross-examination today. It is humanly impossible. I know it's a disappointment to the Trial Chamber. I know there may be some contention as to whether I'm efficient or nonefficient. God knows I'm trying every possible style of cross-examination I can think of. But I would venture to say a full day tomorrow, a full day tomorrow, will absolutely be necessary. And I don't want to guarantee that I will be finished. But that's the matter I wish to bring to the Court's attention. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let me turn to the Prosecution to see whether there's any reactions from their side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I at this point object to the use of a document that has not been translated. In addition, a document from a witness statement is -- information in it is fair game. And I think counsel should be able to ask whatever questions he thinks are relevant from the information in a document. However, the Republika Srpska government has denied Srebrenica happened, has said in an official document that the Muslims killed themselves. Almost to a man every Republika Srpska soldier we have talked to has denied taking part in this or that it occurred, so if there's one statement where a person denies being involved in it, I think we need to be careful in making much of these actual statements before they are translated. But the information inside the statement, anything that Mr. Karnavas has learned that is relevant, I think yes, he has a right to ask and cross-examine the witness on that, and I don't have any problem on that. I would like to see it come to an end. He has had lots of time to cross-examine him. He is well over the time the Prosecution took, or certainly will be by the end of the day. And -- but we remain flexible to what the Court feels is the best way to go forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any response, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I guess I do need to respond a little bit. And I'm trying to exercise my breathing at this point because I think remarks such as attacks on the Republika Srpska are unhelpful. And Mr. McCloskey knows that there has been a change of government in the Republika Srpska. And this year, in particular, during the anniversary, they went over there. So I think it's unhelpful, and he's on record making comments such as the people in that part of the world do not act in a civilised manner. I don't think --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I object to that. I'm sorry to engage in this, but that's just such malarky.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's on the record, Your Honour. And I've stated many times in my motions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm asking your comments about whether you could introduce this document or not, only this issue, but not an overall assessment of what the Prosecution said. I think we could make our own judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, as far as I can understand it, I can confront a witness with anything just about. Now, whether I can actually have it admitted into evidence may be a different matter. There, I need to lay a foundation. Now, I am prepared to have the registry fly my investigator here. I am prepared to fly the gentleman over here to lay a foundation if necessary. The gentleman has indicated that he's prepared to testify in Court. Now, the Prosecutor has indicated that we've gone well over our period of time. I think that's unhelpful as well because I would say I'm being allotted half the time that he was allotted to prepare this witness. So numbers don't get us anywhere. But as far as me having the ability to show this to the witness and to say: "What do you say now, now that you're being confronted with this, do you agree or do you deny?"
